title: Racing: The Need for Speed
summary: Almost as soon as cars existed, people wanted to know which one was fastest. The first races ran along ordinary country roads from one city to another, until they became far too dangerous and moved onto special tracks. Racing drivers chased speed records all the way to a jet car that went faster than sound, and many of the tricks they learned now keep your family car safe.

sections.heading: A Newspaper Invents the Motor Race
paragraphs: Imagine standing at the edge of a dusty road just outside Paris on the morning of 22 July 1894. Crowds line the route in their summer hats. Bicycles weave between the spectators. Then, one by one, a strange parade of machines rattles past: little petrol carriages with tall wooden wheels, a few steam vehicles hissing and puffing, and drivers in caps and goggles gripping steering tillers. This was Paris–Rouen, and it is often called the world's first motor competition.

It was not organised by a carmaker or a sports club, but by a newspaper. Le Petit Journal, one of the most popular papers in France, was always looking for exciting stories that would sell more copies. Its editor, Pierre Giffard, had already organised famous bicycle races. Now he announced a contest for 'horseless carriages' from Paris to the city of Rouen, a distance of about 126 kilometres (78 miles) along the valley of the River Seine.

The interest was astonishing for such a new invention. More than a hundred people paid the entry fee, and their ideas for powering a vehicle were wonderfully varied. Some entries were said to run on compressed air, on gravity, on levers or even on weights and pendulums. Most of those never turned up. To make sure only real working machines started, the organisers held short qualifying runs of about 50 kilometres in the days before the main event. In the end, 21 vehicles lined up for the start.

Here is an important detail: Paris–Rouen was not really meant to be a race. The main prize of 5,000 francs was to go to the vehicle that came 'closest to the ideal', which the judges defined as safe, easy to control and cheap to run. Speed mattered, but so did reliability. This made sense in 1894. Most people had never seen a car, and the big question was not 'How fast can it go?' but 'Will it get there at all?'

The first vehicle to arrive in Rouen was a big steam tractor driven by Count Jules-Albert de Dion, pulling a passenger carriage behind it like a small train on the road. It took about 6 hours and 48 minutes, an average of roughly 19 km/h. But the judges did not give de Dion the top prize. His machine needed a stoker, a second person to shovel fuel into the fire, so it did not fit their idea of a practical everyday vehicle. He received the second prize instead.

Just a few minutes behind came Albert Lemaître in a small Peugeot petrol car. The 5,000-franc prize was shared between two French companies whose cars both used engines built under licence from Gottlieb Daimler: Panhard et Levassor and the Peugeot family firm. Every one of the petrol cars that started reached Rouen, which was a big advertisement for the young petrol engine. The newspapers were full of the story, and a new sport had been born almost by accident.

sections.heading: Levassor's Marathon: Paris to Bordeaux and Back
paragraphs: One year later, the organisers went further. On 11 June 1895 the cars set out on Paris–Bordeaux–Paris, a giant loop of about 1,178 kilometres (732 miles) from the capital down to the port of Bordeaux in south-west France and back again. This time it really was a race: the fastest finisher would be the winner, though the prize rules still had a catch, as we will see.

The star of the event was Émile Levassor, one of the two partners of Panhard et Levassor. He was a 52-year-old engineer, and he drove a two-seater Panhard with an engine of about 1.2 litres, producing only a few horsepower. Today a small family hatchback has about twenty times more power. His car had solid rubber tyres, no windscreen and no roof. At night the road ahead was lit only by dim lamps.

Levassor drove through the day, through the night and into the next day. According to the story usually told, a relief driver had been arranged to take over partway along the route, but Levassor arrived so far ahead of schedule that the man was not ready, so he simply carried on himself. Whether every detail of that story is exact, it is clear that he did nearly all the driving alone. He crossed the finish line in Paris after about 48 hours and 48 minutes, having averaged roughly 24 km/h (15 mph). He was almost six hours ahead of the next car.

Think about what that means. Twenty-four kilometres an hour is about the speed of a fast bicycle rider today. But Levassor kept it up for two days and two nights over roads made for horses, with dust in his eyes and a vibrating, roaring engine in front of him. When he finally climbed down, he is said to have been exhausted but delighted. A monument to him and his drive still stands at the Porte Maillot in Paris.

Here comes the catch. The official rules had been written for four-seater cars, and Levassor's car had only two seats. So the judges did not give him the official first prize. It went instead to Paul Koechlin in a Peugeot, who arrived about eleven hours after Levassor. Many people felt this was unfair, and the following year's big race, Paris–Marseille–Paris in 1896, was simply won by whoever was fastest.

The 1895 race also had a famous loser. André and Édouard Michelin, two brothers who made rubber products, entered a car called L'Éclair fitted with their new air-filled tyres. They suffered puncture after puncture and did not finish within the time limit. (Part 9 tells the story of their tyres.) Still, many people noticed how much more comfortably an air-filled tyre rode over bumps, and within a few years nearly every racing car used them.

Sadly, the dangers of racing caught up with Levassor himself. In the 1896 Paris–Marseille–Paris race he was injured when his car overturned, reportedly after swerving to avoid a dog. He died the following year, in 1897, and many accounts link his death to those injuries. He had helped show the world what a car could do, but his story was an early warning about what speed could cost.

sections.heading: Paris–Madrid: The Race That Had to Stop
paragraphs: Over the next few years, city-to-city racing became wildly popular across Europe. Each year the cars got bigger, heavier and far more powerful. In 1894 the fastest cars averaged under 20 km/h. By 1903 the biggest racing machines could reach well over 120 km/h on a straight road, with engines many times larger than Levassor's. Organisers even introduced a weight limit of 1,000 kilograms for the largest class, so builders stripped their cars down to bare frames to fit in as big an engine as possible.

The roads, however, had not changed much. They were narrow, made of packed gravel or stone, and full of bends, bridges, railway crossings and villages. There were no crash barriers. Animals wandered across. Most dangerous of all, crowds of spectators stood right at the edge of the road, sometimes stepping out to get a better look at the next car coming through the dust.

On 24 May 1903 the most ambitious race of all set off from Versailles, near Paris. Paris–Madrid was meant to run all the way across France and Spain to the Spanish capital. Accounts differ, but somewhere between about 220 and 275 cars and motorcycles started, leaving at intervals from around a quarter to four in the morning. Hundreds of thousands of people were said to be watching along the route.

The dust thrown up by each car hung in the air and made it almost impossible for the next driver to see. Cars overtook one another blindly in thick clouds. Through the day there were a series of terrible crashes. Accounts vary, but somewhere between six and eight people died, including drivers, riding mechanics and spectators, and many more were injured.

One of those killed was Marcel Renault, who with his brothers Louis and Fernand had founded the Renault car company. His car left the road near the village of Couhé-Vérac. His brother Louis, driving another Renault, reached Bordeaux and won the class for lighter cars, only to learn the news of Marcel's accident afterwards. It was a heartbreaking moment for the young company.

The French government acted that same evening. The race was stopped at Bordeaux, the end of the first stage, and was not allowed to continue to Spain. According to many accounts, the cars were not even allowed to drive themselves back. They were pulled to the railway station by horses and sent home to Paris on trains. Fernand Gabriel, in a Mors, was declared the winner of the stage, having averaged around 105 km/h on public roads, an incredible speed for the time.

Paris–Madrid is remembered as the last of the great city-to-city races on open roads. It showed, in the saddest possible way, that fast cars and crowds of people on ordinary roads did not mix. If racing was going to survive, it needed a new home.

sections.heading: Racing Moves Behind the Fences
paragraphs: Some races still used closed-off public roads for a while, with the roads shut and guarded on race day. The first French Grand Prix in 1906, held on a long loop of roads near Le Mans, worked this way. But a few people had a bolder idea: why not build a special place just for fast cars?

In England, the answer came from a wealthy landowner named Hugh Locke King. British law at the time limited cars on public roads to 20 miles per hour, so British carmakers had nowhere to test their cars at full speed. Locke King decided to build a track on his own land at Brooklands, near Weybridge in Surrey. Work began in late 1906, and Brooklands opened on 17 June 1907. It was the world's first purpose-built motor racing circuit.

Brooklands was a giant concrete oval about 4.45 kilometres (2.77 miles) around, 30 metres wide, with huge curved banks at the ends that rose nearly 9 metres high in places. The idea of the banking was like a cyclist leaning into a corner: by tilting the road, the track helped the cars stay on course at high speed without skidding outwards. Painted down the middle was a line that was supposed to show where a car could go round the banking at speed almost without steering. Brooklands could hold huge crowds and also became one of Britain's first airfields; later, famous aircraft were built there. Part of the site is now the Brooklands Museum.

Across the Atlantic, the American businessman Carl G. Fisher had visited European races and wanted something similar at home. (He was the same man who later promoted the Lincoln Highway, as you saw in Part 13.) With three partners he bought farmland outside Indianapolis, Indiana, and built the Indianapolis Motor Speedway, a rectangle with rounded corners exactly 2.5 miles (about 4 kilometres) around. It opened in August 1909.

The first surface was a mix of crushed stone, gravel and tar, and it was a disaster. During the first car races that August it broke up, throwing stones and dust, and several people were killed, including drivers, riding mechanics and spectators. Fisher and his partners quickly decided to repave the whole track with bricks. About 3.2 million bricks, each weighing about 4.5 kilograms (10 pounds), were laid in just a couple of months. That is why the Speedway is still nicknamed 'the Brickyard'. Today the track is covered in asphalt, except for a strip of original bricks one yard wide across the start-finish line, which winning drivers traditionally kneel down and kiss.

sections.heading: Three Great Races: Indy, Le Mans and Formula One
paragraphs: On 30 May 1911 the Speedway held its first 500-mile race: 200 laps of the brick oval. An estimated 80,000 to 85,000 people came to watch, an enormous crowd for the time, and 40 cars started. In those days most racing cars carried two people. Beside the driver sat a riding mechanic, who pumped oil by hand, watched the tyres and, very importantly, turned round to warn the driver about cars coming up from behind.

Ray Harroun, a 32-year-old engineer, drove a long, pointed yellow car called the Marmon Wasp, built by the Nordyke and Marmon company of Indianapolis. His car had only one seat, and other teams complained that a driver alone could not safely see what was behind him. Harroun's answer was to fix a small mirror on a frame above the cockpit so he could glance back at the cars following him. It is believed to be one of the first rear-view mirrors ever used on a car. Harroun later admitted that on the bumpy bricks the mirror shook so much that it was not very useful, but the idea caught on, and today every car on the road has one.

Harroun drove carefully, saving his tyres, while faster rivals stopped again and again to change theirs. A relief driver, Cyrus Patschke, took the wheel for a stretch of about 35 laps in the middle of the race. Harroun won in 6 hours, 42 minutes and 8 seconds, averaging about 74.6 mph (120 km/h). The Indianapolis 500 has been held almost every year since, apart from wartime breaks, and is one of the most famous races in the world.

In France, a different kind of challenge appeared in 1923. On 26 and 27 May, cars raced around a loop of closed public roads near the town of Le Mans for a whole day and a whole night: the first 24 Hours of Le Mans. The point was not just to be fast but to be tough. Lights had to work through the dark, brakes had to last, and engines had to keep running hour after hour. The first winners were André Lagache and René Léonard in a Chenard et Walcker, sharing the driving between them.

Le Mans is still held every year, today on the Circuit de la Sarthe, which is about 13.6 kilometres long and still partly made of public roads that are closed for the race. For many years the race began with the famous 'Le Mans start': drivers stood on one side of the track, ran across when the flag dropped, jumped into their cars and roared away. Because drivers sometimes set off before fastening their safety belts, this start was dropped in 1970 and replaced the next year by a rolling start. In 2010, the winning car covered about 5,410 kilometres in 24 hours, almost as far as a flight from Paris to New York.

Grand Prix racing (from the French for 'great prize') continued through the 1920s and 1930s with fierce battles between teams from Italy, France, Germany and Britain. After the Second World War, the sport's governing body created a single set of rules, known as Formula One, and in 1950 started a World Championship for drivers. The very first championship race was the British Grand Prix at Silverstone, a former wartime airfield in the English countryside, on 13 May 1950. King George VI and the royal family came to watch.

That first race was won by the Italian driver Giuseppe 'Nino' Farina in an Alfa Romeo, averaging about 146 km/h over 70 laps. Farina went on to win the 1950 championship, becoming the first Formula One World Champion. Today Formula One cars are among the most advanced machines on Earth, packed with sensors, carbon fibre and hybrid engines, and the championship visits countries on almost every continent.

sections.heading: Faster Than Sound: The Land Speed Record
paragraphs: While racers competed against each other, a few daring drivers competed against the clock. The land speed record is the highest speed ever officially measured for a car. Under the rules, a car has to make two runs in opposite directions over a measured distance, usually a kilometre or a mile, within a short time limit, and the official speed is the average of the two. This cancels out any help from wind or a gentle slope.

The very first records were set in France in 1898 and 1899 by electric cars. Count Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat set the first official record of about 63 km/h in December 1898, and in 1899 Camille Jenatzy's bullet-shaped electric car became the first to pass 100 km/h (Part 7 tells that story). Petrol cars took over from 1902, though a Stanley steam car snatched the record in 1906.

Records soon needed long, flat, open spaces. Drivers raced along beaches at low tide, such as Pendine Sands in Wales and Daytona Beach in Florida, and later on the dazzling white Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, a dried-up lake bed so flat you can see the curve of the Earth.

The British driver Malcolm Campbell became the most famous record-breaker of the 1920s and 1930s. He named his cars Blue Bird after seeing a play called The Blue Bird by the Belgian writer Maurice Maeterlinck, and painted them blue. Between 1924 and 1935 he set nine land speed records. His first, in 1924 at Pendine Sands, was about 146 mph (235 km/h). On 3 September 1935, at Bonneville, he became the first person to drive a car faster than 300 mph (about 484 km/h). He also set speed records on water in boats called Blue Bird, and his son Donald carried on the family tradition.

After the Second World War, record cars changed completely. Wheel-driven cars with giant piston engines, like John Cobb's Railton, which reached about 394 mph in 1947, gave way to cars pushed along by jet engines from aircraft. In 1963 the American Craig Breedlove drove a three-wheeled jet car, Spirit of America, past 400 mph. In 1970 a rocket car called Blue Flame passed 1,000 km/h. In 1983 the British businessman Richard Noble drove his jet car Thrust2 to about 633 mph (1,019 km/h) in Nevada.

Noble's next dream was even bigger: a car that would break the sound barrier. The speed of sound in air at ground level is roughly 1,200 km/h, depending on the temperature. Going faster than that on land was risky in ways nobody fully understood. Shock waves might lift the car off the ground or batter it apart. The team built ThrustSSC (SSC stands for 'supersonic car'), designed by Ron Ayers, Glynne Bowsher and others.

ThrustSSC looked like a jet fighter without wings. It was about 16.5 metres long, weighed about 10.6 tonnes and was pushed by two Rolls-Royce Spey jet engines of the kind used in Phantom fighter planes, producing around 50,000 pounds of thrust at full power. At top speed it burned roughly 18 litres of fuel every second. Its driver was Andy Green, a Royal Air Force fighter pilot, chosen because he was used to thinking and reacting at enormous speeds.

On 15 October 1997, in the Black Rock Desert of Nevada, Green made two runs in opposite directions and set a record of about 1,228 km/h (763 mph). For the first time ever, a car on the ground had gone faster than sound, and observers heard the sonic boom roll across the desert. The record still stands today. ThrustSSC now rests in the Coventry Transport Museum in England. From Chasseloup-Laubat's 63 km/h to Green's 1,228 km/h, the record grew almost twentyfold in a century.

sections.heading: From the Racetrack to Your Driveway
paragraphs: Carmakers have long said that racing improves the breed, meaning that the hard lessons of the racetrack find their way into ordinary cars. That is not always true, but in some important cases it is.

The clearest example is the disc brake. Early cars used drum brakes, where curved shoes press outwards against the inside of a metal drum turning with the wheel. They work, but when they get very hot after repeated hard stops, they lose grip, a problem called brake fade. A disc brake instead squeezes pads against both sides of a flat metal disc, a bit like pinching a spinning coin between your fingers. The disc is out in the open air, so it cools much faster.

In 1953 Jaguar, working with the Dunlop company, raced its C-Type sports cars at Le Mans with disc brakes on all four wheels. While other drivers had to brake early and carefully to save their overheating brakes, the Jaguar drivers could brake later and harder lap after lap. Jaguar C-Types finished first, second and fourth, and the winners, Duncan Hamilton and Tony Rolt, became the first to win Le Mans at an average of over 100 mph. Other carmakers took note. The Citroën DS of 1955 had front disc brakes, and within a couple of decades they were common on everyday cars. Most new cars today have discs at least on the front wheels.

Racing also taught engineers about tyres, which had to grip at high speed without overheating or bursting, and about aerodynamics, the science of how air flows around a moving object. Racing teams used wind tunnels to make cars slipperier and, from the late 1960s, fitted wings that use the air rushing past to push the car down onto the road, a bit like an upside-down aeroplane wing. Everyday cars use the same science to save fuel and stay stable on the motorway.

The most important lessons, though, were about safety, and many were learned painfully. On 11 June 1955 at Le Mans, a car crashed into the crowd and more than 80 spectators died. It remains motor racing's worst disaster. Several countries temporarily banned racing, and tracks around the world began building stronger barriers and keeping crowds further back.

In the 1960s, the Scottish Formula One champion Jackie Stewart began campaigning hard for safety after he was trapped in his crashed car at the Belgian Grand Prix in 1966. Partly thanks to campaigners like him, racing gradually adopted full safety harnesses, fireproof suits, better helmets, crash barriers, run-off areas and on-site medical teams. Racing cars were built with strong survival cells around the driver, rather like the rigid passenger compartment you will meet in Part 16. Later came the HANS device, a collar that stops a driver's head whipping forward in a crash, required in Formula One from 2003.

In 2018 Formula One introduced the halo, a curved titanium bar above the cockpit that protects the driver's head from flying wheels and debris. Some people complained that it looked ugly. Then, at the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2020, Romain Grosjean's car hit a barrier and burst into flames. The halo pushed the metal barrier away from his head, and he climbed out of the fire with burns to his hands. Afterwards he said that without the halo he would not have been able to talk about it.

So racing is a story of courage, cleverness and showmanship, but also of risk. Every rule about barriers, belts and helmets exists because someone was hurt or killed before it was made. And as cars on ordinary roads became faster and more common, the same question that haunted racing began to haunt everyday life too.

deepDive: Why did early races matter so much? In the 1890s cars were expensive curiosities, and many people doubted they would ever be more than toys for the rich. Races were public demonstrations. When every petrol car that started Paris–Rouen in 1894 reached the finish, and when Levassor averaged about 24 km/h for 1,178 km in 1895, it proved that petrol cars could be reliable over long distances, at a time when steam and electric cars were still serious rivals. Newspapers and carmakers understood this marketing value immediately, which is why so many early races were organised by publishers and why companies such as Panhard, Peugeot, Mercedes and Renault poured money into them. The land speed record also tells a story about physics. Air resistance (drag) grows roughly with the square of speed, so the power needed to overcome it grows roughly with the cube. Doubling your speed needs around eight times the power to push through the air. That is why records crept up from about 63 km/h to about 100 km/h with modest electric motors, then needed aircraft engines of hundreds of horsepower, and finally jet engines. ThrustSSC's two Spey engines gave around 50,000 pounds of thrust, which engineers often compare to the power of about 100,000 horsepower, or roughly a thousand family cars. Near the speed of sound, air can no longer move out of the way smoothly, and shock waves form. The ThrustSSC team spent years on computer simulations and models to make sure the car would stay on the ground. Historians also debate how much racing really improved ordinary cars. Disc brakes are a strong example, though they had been used on aircraft and a few earlier cars before Jaguar's success. Other technologies, such as safety glass and seatbelts, came mainly from road-safety research rather than racing. Racing's biggest gift may be in safety culture: tragedies such as Paris–Madrid in 1903 and Le Mans in 1955 forced organisers to think systematically about crowds, barriers and the human body, and modern Formula One survival cells and the halo are the result of decades of crash investigation. Finally, a note on the rear-view mirror: Harroun's 1911 mirror is famous, but a few writers mention earlier examples, so it is safest to call it one of the first, not the very first.
funFact: The Indianapolis Motor Speedway was paved with about 3.2 million bricks in 1909, and a one-yard strip of those original bricks still marks the start-finish line today.

check.q: Why did Ray Harroun fit a mirror to his Marmon Wasp in the first Indianapolis 500 in 1911?
check.a: He drove alone without a riding mechanic, so he needed it to see cars coming up behind him

To look at his engine while he was driving
